content: The eradication of fox rabies in Europe has been a significant achievement, with various factors contributing to its success and providing valuable lessons for future efforts. The study by Bourhy et al. (2013) highlights the ecological and evolutionary dynamics of the rabies virus in Europe, emphasizing the importance of understanding these factors for effective control measures. Similarly, Rupprecht et al. (2008) discuss the development of biological tools and strategies for rabies prevention, including oral vaccination campaigns. Nadin-Davis et al. (2012) report the emergence of the Arctic rabies virus lineage, which underscores the need for continuous surveillance and adaptation of control strategies to address evolving viral threats. Kuzmin et al. (2008) further explore the distribution, phylogeny, and evolutionary history of Arctic and Arctic-like rabies viruses, providing insights into their spread and genetic diversity. Gould et al. (2002) describe the characterization of an Australian bat lyssavirus variant isolated from insectivorous bats, highlighting the zoonotic potential of lyssaviruses and the need for vigilance in monitoring bat populations. Vargas-Linares et al. (2014) document rabies cases in Potos flavus in Peru, emphasizing the importance of identifying and addressing rabies reservoirs in wildlife. Aréchiga-Ceballos et al. (2010) identify a new rabies virus variant during an epizootic in white-nosed coatis in the Yucatan Peninsula, demonstrating the role of wildlife in rabies transmission dynamics. Condori-Condori et al. (2013) discuss enzootic and epizootic rabies associated with vampire bats in Peru, highlighting the public health risks posed by these animals. De Serres et al. (2008) analyze bat rabies cases in the United States and Canada, noting human cases with and without direct bat contact, which underscores the need for public awareness and preventive measures. Markotter et al. (2008) examine the epidemiology and pathogenicity of African bat lyssaviruses, emphasizing the importance of understanding regional variations in rabies virus strains. The WHO Technical Report Series No. 1012 (2018) outlines the critical role of surveillance in rabies control and elimination. Effective surveillance involves systematic collection, analysis, and dissemination of health data to monitor disease presence, improve awareness, and document the absence of disease. Surveillance systems must be tailored to public health objectives and the epidemiology of rabies in specific regions. During endemic phases, passive surveillance may suffice to detect cases due to the high incidence of disease. However, as control programs progress, active monitoring becomes essential to verify vaccination coverage and other interventions. The use of gold-standard diagnostic tests and trained personnel is crucial for accurate case detection and management. Surveillance data should inform management decisions and guide interventions. As rabies control activities reduce human cases to zero and eliminate the disease in target animal populations, additional surveillance is necessary to validate and verify these achievements. National notification systems and standardized case definitions are essential for systematic recognition and reporting of suspected cases. Monitoring the use of post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is also critical. Suspected exposures should be assessed according to national protocols, and PEP administration should be documented systematically. Investigations should identify the source of exposure and ensure appropriate follow-up for affected individuals. Optimal surveillance targets all suspected human and animal rabies cases, facilitating systematic recognition and categorization based on clinical, epidemiological, and diagnostic features. Surveillance systems must be supported by appropriate infrastructure, logistics, and public awareness to ensure timely detection and response to rabies cases.
